subject: Science

unit.unitOverview: Open your eyes right now and look around you. Perhaps you can see the sunlight coming through a window, the pages of this book, your own hand, or the face of someone you love. Have you ever stopped to wonder how you are able to see any of it? In this unit you will discover the answer, and it is one of the most wonderful stories in all of science. The answer is light.
learningPath: Preview the goals and core ideas
Learn methods and study worked examples
Complete guided practice, experiments and games
Apply, explain and complete the Unit Challenge

objectives.text: Observe that shadows are formed when light travelling from a source is blocked
Know that we see light sources because light from the source enters our eyes
Know that beams/rays of light can be reflected by surfaces including mirrors, and when reflected light enters our eyes we see the object
Explore why a beam of light changes direction when it is reflected from a surface

objectives.subStrand: Obtain and present evidence; Consider evidence and approach

outcomes: Identify light sources and tell the difference between objects that make their own light and objects that only reflect light.
Explain that light travels in straight lines, and use this idea to explain shadows and why you cannot see around corners.
Describe how you see an object: light travels from a source, bounces off the object, and enters your eye.
Investigate how mirrors reflect light, and use two mirrors to see hidden things.
Classify materials as transparent, translucent, or opaque, and predict the shadows they make.
Name the main parts of the eye and explain, in simple words, how it lets you see.
Recognise that light can bend (refract) when it passes into water, and connect this to why a straw looks broken in a glass.
Apply what you learn to real life: mirrors, safety in bright sun, and clean vision.

concepts.title: Light Sources and How Light Travels
concepts.explanation:
Objects that make light, and objects that only reflect it

Let us begin with a simple question that hides a deep idea. Look around your home and think about everything you can see. Which of those things actually make their own light? The answer is: only a few. The sun blazing over the Rift Valley makes its own light. A candle flame makes its own light. A torch, a cooking fire, a lightning flash, and a glowing phone screen all make their own light. We call all of these light sources.

Now think about everything else: this book, your clothes, a cup, a goat in the yard, a wall, the moon in the night sky. None of these make their own light. You can only see them because light from a light source lands on them and bounces off into your eyes. In a completely dark room they simply vanish from view, even though they are still right there in front of you. This is one of the most important truths in the whole unit, so say it to yourself: most things you see do not glow. They only reflect the light of a true light source.

A famous example is the moon. On a clear night at Berbera the moon can look so bright that it lights the whole beach. Many people think the moon makes its own light, but it does not. The moon is a giant ball of rock with no fire and no flame. It shines only because sunlight travels across space, hits the moon, and reflects back down to us. The moon is a reflector, not a light source, just like a mirror. This same moon marks the beginning of Ramadan and the Islamic months, and now you know the science of why it glows.

Light sources come in two families. Natural light sources are made by nature: the sun, the stars, lightning, and even a few glowing living creatures such as fireflies. Artificial light sources are made by people: torches, electric bulbs, candles, oil lamps, and screens. Both families do the same job. They pour out light energy that then travels across the room and lets you see.

[Did You Know] Did You Know? The sun is so far away that its light takes about eight minutes to reach the Earth. So when you feel the warm morning sun on your face, that light actually left the sun eight minutes earlier. You are always seeing the sun a little bit in the past!

Here is the second great idea of this unit: light travels in straight lines. It does not curve around corners on its own, and it does not bend by itself to find you. Once light leaves a source, it shoots out in perfectly straight paths in every direction. Scientists draw these straight paths as arrows and call each one a ray of light.

How do we know light is straight? You have proof all around you. Think of the beams of sunlight that break through gaps in the clouds during the rainy season, or the straight beam of a torch cutting through a dark room. They are always straight lines, never curves. If you shine a torch through a straight cardboard tube, the light passes right through and comes out the far end. But if you bend that tube into a curve, the light cannot follow the bend, so it strikes the inside wall and no light comes out the other end. The light refuses to turn a corner. You will test this yourself in the Experiments book.

Because light travels straight, it creates shadows. When light streams toward an opaque object such as Yusuf standing in the sun, the light cannot pass through his body and it cannot bend around him. So the ground behind Yusuf is left dark. That dark patch is his shadow. The shape of the shadow matches the shape of the object, because the straight rays are simply blocked. Early in the morning and late in the afternoon, when the sun is low in the sky, shadows stretch out very long across the ground. At midday, when the sun is high overhead, shadows shrink and hide almost under your feet. The shadow moves all day because the sun moves across the sky, changing the direction the straight rays come from.
concepts.example: The straight-line rule also explains why you cannot see around a corner. If someone is hiding behind a wall, the light bouncing off them travels in straight lines, and every one of those lines is stopped by the wall. None of them can bend around to reach your eye. This is exactly why a driver on the road to Nairobi needs a mirror to see the traffic behind, and why you will soon learn to use mirrors to peek around corners safely.

concepts.title: How We See Things
concepts.explanation:
Now we can put the pieces together and answer the big question: how do you actually see? Many children (and even many grown-ups) secretly believe that seeing works like a beam shooting out of your eyes onto an object, the way a torch shines. This is completely wrong, and proving it wrong is one of the joys of this unit. Your eyes do not send out any light at all. Your eyes are catchers, not throwers.

Here is what really happens, step by step, when Khadija looks at a ripe red mango on the table:

Light leaves a light source, for example the sun through the window or the lamp above the table.

That light travels in straight lines and lands on the mango.

The mango's skin reflects some of that light. It bounces off in many directions.

Some of the reflected light happens to travel straight into Khadija's eyes.

Her eyes turn that light into signals, and her brain reads the signals as the picture of a red mango.

Notice that light must make a full journey: source, then object, then eye. If any part of that journey is missing, you see nothing. Turn off every light in the room and the mango disappears, not because it moved, but because there is no light to reflect off it and reach your eyes. This is why you cannot read the Qur'an in a pitch-black room no matter how hard you stare, and why a small oil lamp or torch instantly makes the words appear.

Why is the mango red and the leaf green? White light from the sun is actually a mixture of all colours mixed together. When white light hits the mango, the skin soaks up (absorbs) most colours but bounces back the red light. That reflected red light reaches your eyes, so you see red. The leaf bounces back green and absorbs the rest, so you see green. The colour you see is simply the colour of light an object reflects best. This is also why a red dress can look dull and almost black under a blue light: there is no red light for it to bounce back.

[Did You Know] Did You Know? Light is the fastest thing in the whole universe. Nothing can travel faster. In just one second, light could zip around the entire Earth about seven and a half times. That is why the moment you uncover a torch, the far wall lights up instantly with no waiting.

Your eye is a marvel. It is a soft ball, a little smaller than a table-tennis ball, and it is beautifully designed to catch light and turn it into pictures. Let us meet its main parts.

The cornea is the clear, curved window at the very front of your eye. Light enters here first, and the cornea starts to bend the light to aim it inward.

The pupil is the black circle in the middle. It is really a hole that lets light into the eye. In bright sunlight the pupil shrinks small to let in less light; in a dark room it opens wide to catch as much light as possible.

The iris is the coloured ring around the pupil, brown for most of us. It is a tiny muscle that changes the size of the pupil.

The lens sits just behind the pupil. It is clear and it bends the light even more to make a sharp, focused picture.

The retina is the screen at the very back of the eye. The focused light lands here and the retina turns it into nerve signals.

The optic nerve is like a cable that carries those signals to your brain, which reads them as the world you see.
concepts.example: So the full path of seeing is: light enters through the cornea, passes through the pupil, is focused by the lens, lands on the retina, and travels along the optic nerve to the brain. All of this happens faster than you can blink. Watch your own pupils in a mirror: step into a bright doorway and they shrink; step into shade and they open wide. That is your iris protecting your retina by controlling how much light gets in.

concepts.title: Reflection and Mirrors
concepts.explanation:
You already know that light bounces, or reflects, off objects. Most surfaces are slightly rough, so they scatter the light in every direction. That is why you can see this page from any angle but you cannot see your face in it. A mirror is different. A mirror is extremely smooth and shiny, so it reflects nearly all the light in a neat, orderly way. The rays stay organised, so instead of a blur you see a clear picture, an image.

Nature makes mirrors too. On a calm, windless morning, the surface of a pond, a water bucket, or a quiet part of the Indian Ocean near Lamu can become as smooth as glass. Look down and you will see the sky, the palm trees, and your own face reflected perfectly. But throw a stone in, or let the wind ripple the water, and the reflection breaks into a shimmering mess. Why? Because the once-smooth surface is now bumpy and tilted in a thousand directions, so it scatters the light instead of reflecting it in an orderly way. Still water is a mirror; choppy water is not. Remember this example, because it explains a great deal.

There is a neat rule for how light bounces off a mirror. The light comes in at some angle and leaves at the same angle on the other side, like a football bouncing off a smooth wall. Scientists say 'the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection', which simply means the bounce is even and predictable. Because the bounce is predictable, you can aim reflected light exactly where you want it. If Idris tilts a small mirror in the sun, he can send a bright spot of sunlight dancing onto the ceiling or across the yard, steering it wherever he points the mirror.

This predictable bounce is what makes mirrors so useful. With a single mirror you can see your own face, check behind your headscarf, or watch a doorway you are not facing. With two mirrors you can do something even cleverer: see around a corner or over a wall. This is exactly how a periscope works. A periscope is a tall tube with a mirror at the top and a mirror at the bottom, each tilted. Light from above bounces off the top mirror, travels straight down the tube, bounces off the bottom mirror, and comes out to your eye. Sailors in submarines use periscopes to see above the water while staying safely below. You will build a simple one at home.
concepts.example: [Did You Know] Did You Know? Car mirrors, security mirrors in shops, and the round mirror at a blind road junction are often gently curved outward. A curved mirror squeezes a very wide view into a small space, so a driver can see many cars and people at once. That is why the mirror often says that objects are closer than they appear.

concepts.title: Transparent, Translucent, and Opaque Materials
concepts.explanation:
Not everything treats light the same way. Some things let light pour straight through, some let a little through, and some stop it completely. Scientists sort materials into three groups based on how they handle light.

A transparent material lets almost all the light pass straight through, so you can see clearly through it. Clear window glass is transparent, and so is clean water in a glass and clear plastic wrap. That is why houses have glass windows: they let the daylight flood in while keeping out the wind, rain, dust, and insects. You can look right through and see the street outside.

A translucent material lets some light through but scatters it, so the light that comes out is soft and blurry and you cannot see clearly through it. Thin cloth, wax paper, frosted bathroom glass, and a thin plastic bottle are translucent. Hold your hand behind a translucent curtain and you see only a fuzzy dark shape, not your fingers. This is very useful. A bathroom window can be made of frosted glass so that daylight comes in but no one outside can see in, giving privacy. A lampshade is often translucent so it softens a harsh bulb into a gentle glow.

An opaque material blocks light completely. No light passes through at all. Wood, metal, cardboard, thick cloth, stone, and your own body are all opaque. Because opaque objects stop light, they are the ones that cast dark, sharp shadows. A wooden door is opaque, which is why a room with the door shut and no window can be pitch dark in the middle of the day.
concepts.example: You can even tell which group a material belongs to by looking at the shadow it casts. Shine a torch at each one against a wall. A transparent material casts almost no shadow, because the light goes right through. A translucent material casts a faint, grey, fuzzy shadow, because it lets some light through and blocks the rest. An opaque material casts a dark, sharp shadow, because it blocks all the light. So the shadow is a clue to the material.

concepts.title: Bending Light (Refraction)
concepts.explanation:
You have learned that light travels in straight lines. That is true, but there is one important situation where light changes direction: when it passes from one clear material into another, such as from air into water. This bending of light is called refraction, and it leads to some surprising sights.

Try this in your mind, and later with a real glass. Put a straight straw or a pencil into a clear glass of water and look from the side. The straw appears to bend or break right at the surface of the water. Lift it out and it is perfectly straight again. The straw never actually bends, of course. What bends is the light. Light travelling from the underwater part of the straw slows down and changes direction as it leaves the water and enters the air, so it reaches your eye from a slightly different angle. Your brain assumes light always came straight, so it draws the straw in the wrong place, and the straw looks broken.
concepts.example: Refraction happens all around the coast and the rivers. If Sagal tries to grab a fish she sees in the shallow water of the Jubba River, the fish is not exactly where it appears to be; refraction has shifted its apparent position, so she must aim a little differently. A coin at the bottom of a bucket of water looks closer to the surface than it really is, for the same reason. Even a beautiful rainbow after the rains is made by sunlight refracting and splitting into colours inside tiny raindrops. Refraction is also the reason spectacles work: a curved lens bends light in just the right way to make a blurry world sharp again for people who need help seeing.

concepts.title: Guided Exploration - Think It Through
concepts.explanation:
Work through these questions slowly. They are not a test. They are here to help your understanding grow. Say your answers out loud or write them in your notebook, then talk them over with your AI tutor or your teacher.

You are sitting in a room with the curtains closed and no lamp on. It is completely dark. A red ball is on the floor right in front of you. Why can you not see it, and what is the smallest change that would let you see it?

Two children argue. Amina says 'we see the moon because it makes its own light.' Omar says 'no, the moon only reflects the sun.' Who is right, and how would you explain the answer kindly to the other?

Draw arrows to show the path of light that lets you see a white cup on a table under a lamp. Where does the light start, where does it go, and where does it end?

Your friend covers a torch with clear plastic, then with wax paper, then with cardboard. Predict what the shadow on the wall looks like in each case, and say why.

You want to watch the door behind you while you keep facing your book. Describe how a single mirror could help, and where you would place it.
concepts.example: Explain why still water at dawn shows a clear reflection but the same water shows no reflection when the wind makes waves.

methods.title: Light Source or Reflector?
methods.example: To find out which objects in your home make their own light and which only reflect light from another source.
steps: In a normal lit room, list ten objects you can see.
Now make the room as dark as you can. Which objects can you still see glowing on their own? Write them down.
Turn on only the torch. Notice that the mirror, the paper, and other objects suddenly appear again because they reflect the torchlight.
Cover the torch completely with your hand. Notice everything vanishes again.
Sort your ten objects into two columns: makes its own light and only reflects light.

methods.title: Does Light Travel in Straight Lines?
methods.example: To prove that light travels in straight lines and cannot bend around corners on its own.
steps: Shine the torch through the straight tube and look at the far end. Record what you see.
Gently bend the tube into a curve and shine the torch again. Record what happens.
Make a small hole in the centre of each of the three cardboard pieces.
Stand them up in a row, about a hand-width apart, so the three holes line up straight. Shine the torch through the first hole and see if light reaches the far side.
Slide the middle card sideways so its hole is no longer in line. Shine again and record.

methods.title: The Bending Straw (Refraction)
methods.example: To observe refraction, the bending of light, and see why a straw looks broken in water.
steps: Fill the clear glass about three-quarters full with clean water.
Put the straw into the water and look at the glass from the side, at the level of the water surface.
Notice how the straw appears to bend or break at the water line. Draw exactly what you see.
Slowly lift the straw out and see that it was straight all along.
Extra test: place a coin at the bottom of the empty glass, step back until it just disappears behind the rim, then have someone pour in water. Watch the coin seem to rise into view.

methods.title: Mirror Magic and a Simple Periscope
methods.example: To explore how mirrors reflect light and to build a two-mirror periscope that lets you see over or around something.
steps: First, explore one mirror: shine the torch at it from different angles and watch where the reflected spot lands on the wall. Notice the light bounces off at the same angle it arrived.
Cut a viewing hole near the top of one side of the box and another near the bottom of the opposite side.
Tape one mirror at the top, tilted at a slant, facing the top hole.
Tape the second mirror at the bottom, tilted the opposite way, facing the bottom hole.
Look into the bottom hole. You should be able to see over the top, as if you were taller. Aim it round a doorway or over a wall.

methods.title: Transparent, Translucent, or Opaque?
methods.example: To classify household materials by how much light they let through, and to link each type to the shadow it makes.
steps: Darken the room a little so shadows show clearly.
Hold the first material between the torch and the wall.
Observe how much light passes through and what kind of shadow appears on the wall.
Decide: transparent (clear shadow-free), translucent (fuzzy grey shadow), or opaque (dark sharp shadow).
Repeat for every material and fill in your table.

workedExamples.title: Tracing a Light Path
workedExamples.prompt: Some science needs careful step-by-step thinking, just like a maths problem. Here is a worked example of tracing the path of light so you can see an object. Follow every step.
workedExamples.solution:
Problem: Halima is sitting in the evening. There is a lamp on the shelf. On the table there is a yellow banana. Halima can see the banana clearly. Draw and describe the complete path of the light, step by step.

Step 1 — Find the light source. Nothing can be seen without a source. The banana does not glow, and Halima's eyes do not shine. The only source here is the lamp. So the light story must begin at the lamp.

Step 2 — Light travels in straight lines to the object. Light leaves the lamp and shoots out in straight rays in all directions. Some of those rays travel straight to the banana. Draw a straight arrow from the lamp to the banana.

Step 3 — The object reflects the light. The banana skin absorbs most colours but reflects yellow light. That yellow light bounces off in many directions. Draw arrows spreading out from the banana.

workedExamples.title: Which of these is a light source
workedExamples.prompt: Which of these is a light source? (a) a mirror (b) the moon (c) a candle flame (d) a white wall
workedExamples.solution: c) a candle flame A candle makes its own light; the others only reflect.

workedExamples.title: Light travels in
workedExamples.prompt: Light travels in: (a) curved lines (b) straight lines (c) zigzags (d) circles
workedExamples.solution: b) straight lines This is a basic property of light.

workedExamples.title: We can see the moon at night because it
workedExamples.prompt: We can see the moon at night because it: (a) makes its own light (b) reflects sunlight (c) glows in the dark (d) is on fire
workedExamples.solution: b) reflects sunlight The moon is a reflector, not a light source.

workedExamples.title: We see a book because light
workedExamples.prompt: We see a book because light: (a) goes from our eyes to the book (b) is made by the book (c) reflects off the book into our eyes (d) bends around the book
workedExamples.solution: c) reflects off the book into our eyes Eyes catch light; they do not send it.

workedExamples.title: A material that lets no light through is
workedExamples.prompt: A material that lets no light through is: (a) transparent (b) translucent (c) opaque (d) reflective
workedExamples.solution: c) opaque Opaque means no light passes through.

workedExamples.title: Frosted bathroom glass is best described as
workedExamples.prompt: Frosted bathroom glass is best described as: (a) transparent (b) translucent (c) opaque (d) a light source
workedExamples.solution: b) translucent Frosted glass scatters light so you cannot see clearly.

workedExamples.title: A straw looks bent in water because light
workedExamples.prompt: A straw looks bent in water because light: (a) reflects (b) refracts (bends) (c) stops (d) speeds up forever
workedExamples.solution: b) refracts (bends) Light bends leaving the water, so the straw looks bent.

activities.title: Light Source or Reflector?
activities.materials: A torch; A mirror; A phone or screen (with permission); A sheet of white paper; A dark room, such as a store-room at night, or a cupboard
steps: In a normal lit room, list ten objects you can see.
Now make the room as dark as you can. Which objects can you still see glowing on their own? Write them down.
Turn on only the torch. Notice that the mirror, the paper, and other objects suddenly appear again because they reflect the torchlight.
Cover the torch completely with your hand. Notice everything vanishes again.
Sort your ten objects into two columns: makes its own light and only reflects light.
Safety: Glass breaks — carry jars and mirrors with two hands, and tell an adult straight away if anything chips or cracks.

activities.title: Does Light Travel in Straight Lines?
activities.materials: A torch; A cardboard tube (from kitchen roll), or a rolled sheet of cardboard; Three pieces of cardboard about the size of your hand; A pencil to make holes; A piece of string; A dark room
steps: Shine the torch through the straight tube and look at the far end. Record what you see.
Gently bend the tube into a curve and shine the torch again. Record what happens.
Make a small hole in the centre of each of the three cardboard pieces.
Stand them up in a row, about a hand-width apart, so the three holes line up straight. Shine the torch through the first hole and see if light reaches the far side.
Slide the middle card sideways so its hole is no longer in line. Shine again and record.

activities.title: The Bending Straw (Refraction)
activities.materials: A clear glass or jar; Clean water; A straight straw, a pencil, or a long spoon; A coin (for the extra test)
steps: Fill the clear glass about three-quarters full with clean water.
Put the straw into the water and look at the glass from the side, at the level of the water surface.
Notice how the straw appears to bend or break at the water line. Draw exactly what you see.
Slowly lift the straw out and see that it was straight all along.
Extra test: place a coin at the bottom of the empty glass, step back until it just disappears behind the rim, then have someone pour in water. Watch the coin seem to rise into view.

activities.title: Mirror Magic and a Simple Periscope
activities.materials: Two small mirrors (plastic if possible); A torch; A long cardboard box or a tall milk carton; Tape; Scissors (ask an adult to help cut)
steps: First, explore one mirror: shine the torch at it from different angles and watch where the reflected spot lands on the wall. Notice the light bounces off at the same angle it arrived.
Cut a viewing hole near the top of one side of the box and another near the bottom of the opposite side.
Tape one mirror at the top, tilted at a slant, facing the top hole.
Tape the second mirror at the bottom, tilted the opposite way, facing the bottom hole.
Look into the bottom hole. You should be able to see over the top, as if you were taller. Aim it round a doorway or over a wall.
Safety: Glass breaks — carry jars and mirrors with two hands, and tell an adult straight away if anything chips or cracks.

activities.title: Transparent, Translucent, or Opaque?
activities.materials: A torch; A white wall or sheet of paper as a screen; Clear plastic wrap; Wax or greaseproof paper, or thin cloth; Aluminium foil or cardboard; Any other materials you are curious about
steps: Darken the room a little so shadows show clearly.
Hold the first material between the torch and the wall.
Observe how much light passes through and what kind of shadow appears on the wall.
Decide: transparent (clear shadow-free), translucent (fuzzy grey shadow), or opaque (dark sharp shadow).
Repeat for every material and fill in your table.

activities.title: Observe: Guided Exploration - Think It Through
activities.materials: A torch; A mirror; A phone or screen (with permission); A sheet of white paper; A dark room, such as a store-room at night, or a cupboard
steps: Look for an example of guided exploration — think it through around your home or outside.
Watch it closely for a few minutes and note three things you notice.
Write or draw what you observed, using the words Light and Light source.
Explain your finding out loud, as if you were teaching it. Say it to a family member or your teacher if someone is nearby, or explain it to yourself and check it against the concept explanations.

rules.title: Protect Your Eyes
rules.text: Never look straight at the sun, not even for a moment and not even when squinting. The equatorial sun over East Africa is extremely strong, and its light can permanently burn the retina at the back of your eye, harming your sight forever. Wear a hat or use shade at midday, and if you have sunglasses, wear them outdoors. Never stare into a laser pointer or a very bright torch, and never shine one in anyone's eyes. Rest your eyes from screens often, and keep your hands and face clean to protect your eyes from infection and dust.

rules.title: Light Words to Know
rules.text: Remember the key words: source, reflect, transparent, translucent, opaque, refraction.

terms: Light
A form of energy that travels and lets us see.
Light source
An object that makes its own light (sun, candle, torch).
Reflect / Reflection
When light bounces off a surface; also the mirror image.
Ray
A straight line showing the path light travels.
Transparent
Lets almost all light through; you see clearly (glass, water).
Translucent
Lets some scattered light through; you see fuzzily (wax paper).
Opaque
Blocks all light (wood, metal, your body).
Shadow
A dark area where an opaque object blocks the light.
Mirror
A smooth shiny surface that reflects light to form a clear image.
Refraction
The bending of light passing from one clear material into another.
Vision
Seeing, done by the eyes and brain together.
Pupil
The opening that lets light into the eye; changes size with brightness.

vocabulary.meaning: A dark area where an opaque object blocks the light.

vocabulary.meaning: A smooth shiny surface that reflects light to form a clear image.

connections.text: light is one form of energy, like heat and sound; you will meet others in later units.
the eye is a sense organ; plants use light for photosynthesis.
the sun lights the moon and gives us day and night; the new moon marks the Islamic months.
cameras, mirrors, spectacles, screens, and solar panels all use light science.
shadows, angles of reflection, and symmetry link science to drawing and geometry.

realProblems.prompt: Zahra is looking for her sandals in a dark store-room and cannot see them at all. Explain why, and give two ways she could see them.
realProblems.answer: She cannot see because there is no light to reflect off the sandals into her eyes. She could switch on a light or bring a torch, or open a door or window to let daylight in.
realProblems.hint: Decide which idea the situation is about — Light, Light source, Reflect / Reflection — then explain your reasoning step by step.
realProblems.errorFeedback: Check your reasoning against this: She cannot see because there is no light to reflect off the sandals into her eyes. She could switch on a light or bring a torch, or open a door or window to let daylight in.

realProblems.prompt: A driver on the busy road near Eastleigh needs to see cars coming up behind. Explain how mirrors solve this problem using reflection.
realProblems.answer: A mirror reflects the light coming from cars behind and sends it into the driver's eyes, so the driver can see behind without turning around, thanks to reflection.
realProblems.hint: Decide which idea the situation is about — Light, Light source, Reflect / Reflection — then explain your reasoning step by step.
realProblems.errorFeedback: Check your reasoning against this: A mirror reflects the light coming from cars behind and sends it into the driver's eyes, so the driver can see behind without turning around, thanks to reflection.

realProblems.prompt: A family near Mombasa wants daylight in the bathroom but also privacy. What kind of glass should the window be, and why?
realProblems.answer: Frosted (translucent) glass, because it lets daylight into the bathroom while scattering the light so that people outside cannot see clearly through it, giving privacy.
realProblems.hint: Decide which idea the situation is about — Light, Light source, Reflect / Reflection — then explain your reasoning step by step.
realProblems.errorFeedback: Check your reasoning against this: Frosted (translucent) glass, because it lets daylight into the bathroom while scattering the light so that people outside cannot see clearly through it, giving privacy.

realProblems.prompt: Yusuf tries to scoop a fish he sees just under the water of the Jubba River but keeps missing. Explain what is tricking him and how he should adjust.
realProblems.answer: Refraction bends the light coming from the fish as it leaves the water, so the fish is not exactly where it appears. He should aim a little lower or to the side of where he sees it.
realProblems.hint: Decide which idea the situation is about — Light, Light source, Reflect / Reflection — then explain your reasoning step by step.
realProblems.errorFeedback: Check your reasoning against this: Refraction bends the light coming from the fish as it leaves the water, so the fish is not exactly where it appears. He should aim a little lower or to the side of where he sees it.

realProblems.prompt: During a hot, bright afternoon on the savanna, explain why wearing a light-coloured headscarf and a hat helps, using ideas about reflecting and absorbing light and protecting the eyes.
realProblems.answer: Light colours reflect most sunlight and heat away, keeping him cooler, while dark colours absorb it. A hat shades the eyes and face, and keeping the strong sun off the eyes protects the retina from damage.
realProblems.hint: Decide which idea the situation is about — Light, Light source, Reflect / Reflection — then explain your reasoning step by step.
realProblems.errorFeedback: Check your reasoning against this: Light colours reflect most sunlight and heat away, keeping him cooler, while dark colours absorb it. A hat shades the eyes and face, and keeping the strong sun off the eyes protects the retina from damage.

realProblems.prompt: A red apple and a blue book sit under a red light. Predict the colour each appears and explain why, using absorbing and reflecting light.
realProblems.answer: Under red light the red apple still looks red (it reflects red light). The blue book looks dark or black, because there is no blue light for it to reflect and it absorbs the red light.
realProblems.hint: Decide which idea the situation is about — Light, Light source, Reflect / Reflection — then explain your reasoning step by step.
realProblems.errorFeedback: Check your reasoning against this: Under red light the red apple still looks red (it reflects red light). The blue book looks dark or black, because there is no blue light for it to reflect and it absorbs the red light.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: In your own words, what is the difference between a light source and a reflector?
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: A light source makes its own light (sun, candle, torch). A reflector only bounces back light from a source (moon, mirror, paper) and cannot be seen in total darkness.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Explain why light traveling in straight lines causes shadows to form.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: Light cannot bend around an opaque object or pass through it, so the straight rays are blocked and leave a dark shadow shaped like the object behind it.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Describe the complete path of light that lets you see a green leaf in daylight.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: Light from a source (the sun) travels in a straight line to the leaf, reflects off it as green light, travels into the eye, and the brain reads it as a green leaf.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Why does the moon shine even though it has no fire?
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: The moon has no fire of its own; it reflects sunlight that hits it and bounces down to us, like a giant mirror in the sky.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: What is the difference between a translucent and an opaque material? Give one example of each.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: A translucent material lets some scattered light through so you cannot see clearly (example: wax paper or thin cloth). An opaque material lets no light through (example: wood or metal).

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Explain what refraction is and give one everyday example of it.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: Refraction is the bending of light as it passes from one clear material into another, such as air into water. Example: a straw looking bent in a glass of water.

selfAssessment: I can identify light sources and tell the difference between objects that make their own light and objects that only reflect light.
I can explain that light travels in straight lines, and use this idea to explain shadows and why I cannot see around corners.
I can describe how I see an object: light travels from a source, bounces off the object, and enters my eye.
I can investigate how mirrors reflect light, and use two mirrors to see hidden things.
I can classify materials as transparent, translucent, or opaque, and predict the shadows they make.
I can name the main parts of the eye and explain, in simple words, how it lets me see.
I can recognise that light can bend (refract) when it passes into water, and connect this to why a straw looks broken in a glass.
I can apply what I learn to real life: mirrors, safety in bright sun, and clean vision.
